paper_title: Thermal aware task assignment for multicore processors using genetic algorithm

scenario.figure_or_table: Section 5.3.2 and Figure 9 (non-equal initial temperature case), with the setup in Section 5.1 and Figure 6 and the task parameters in Table 1
scenario.description: Thermal-aware GA task assignment on a quad-core out-of-order processor. Task parameters come from gem5 and McPAT. HotSpot gives per-core temperatures over 10 hyper-periods. Initial core temperatures are 65.48, 49.77, 45.82 and 51.86 C with a 45 C ambient. Core temperature is rebalanced; the maximum inter-core difference is about 8 C after the first hyper-period (Figure 10).
scenario.architecture: Quad-core out-of-order CPU with 32 KB I-cache and D-cache, a dedicated 1 MB L2 per core, 64 MB RAM, a DDRx1 memory controller and a 2 GHz clock (Section 5.1, Figure 6). No block floorplan geometry is published.
scenario.workload: 20 independent periodic tasks from SPEC2006, MiBench and MediaBench (Table 1, PDF page 8), with per-task execution time, leakage power, dynamic power and energy.
scenario.operating_point: 2 GHz clock; ambient 45 C; initial core temperatures of 65.48, 49.77, 45.82 and 51.86 C; 10 hyper-periods (about 14 s of simulation, per the abstract and conclusion). The task power values in Table 1 are per task, not per block.

original_setup.solver: HotSpot thermal simulator (compact RC model) driven by gem5 execution times and McPAT task power; the per-core transient temperature is also described by a lumped RC model (Eqs. 1-2), PDF pages 3-7
original_setup.optimizer: Genetic algorithm (binary chromosome, one gene per task, tournament selection, single-point crossover, bitwise mutation, mu+lambda survivor selection) that assigns tasks to cores so each core's energy is about a_j times total energy (Eqs. 8-13, Algorithm-1), PDF pages 5-7
original_setup.controller: Temperature-driven task assignment per hyper-period under EDF scheduling: decision factors a_j are computed from the previous period's steady-state HotSpot core temperatures, with more energy given to cooler cores. This is not a DVFS or closed-loop continuous controller (PDF pages 5-7)
original_setup.benchmark: 20 tasks from SPEC2006, MiBench and MediaBench (Table 1, PDF page 8) on a quad-core out-of-order CPU at 2 GHz. Selected scenario: non-equal initial core temperatures (65.48, 49.77, 45.82, 51.86 C; ambient 45 C) over 10 hyper-periods (Section 5.3.2, Figure 9, PDF page 10)

thermal_observable.location: Maximum temperature difference between cores (inter-core spread) in each hyper-period, Figure 10 (PDF page 10). The paper states roughly 8 C, excluding the first hyper-period where the initial temperatures differ
thermal_observable.aggregation: Maximum inter-core temperature difference per hyper-period over 10 hyper-periods, about 14 s of simulation. The value is approximate and read from the text, not from a tabulated number

physical_mismatches.reason: No block floorplan is published. There are no x, y, width or height values for the cores, L2 caches or other blocks, and Figure 6 is an architecture diagram, not geometry. A steady 2D Studio floorplan therefore cannot be built from the paper without inventing geometry.

Table 1 gives per-task (benchmark) leakage and dynamic power, not per-block power for the same scenario. The paper does not publish a rule for mapping tasks to per-core block power, and the task-to-core assignment per hyper-period is only shown in figures. Total chip power cannot be split into per-block power without inventing a rule.

The original study is transient and scheduling-driven. It uses 10 hyper-periods of about 14 s with core temperatures feeding back into task assignment. A steady 2D thermal solve cannot reproduce the transient peaks or the assignment feedback loop.

The optimizer (GA task assignment) and controller (per-period thermal-aware scheduling under EDF) act on workload allocation, not on a floorplan or package parameters, so they have no counterpart in a static Studio steady-state solve.

The HotSpot package, cooling and material parameters (R and C values, heat sink, TIM, die thickness, ambient coupling beyond the 45 C ambient) are not reported, so the original thermal solver setup is not reproducible.

The system is a planar quad-core CPU with no 3D stacking, interposer or advanced cooling. These are not mismatches with a 2D Studio package, but they confirm that the paper's contribution is scheduling and not geometry.
